blocks.text: Digital footprint and net etiquette

The trail of data that a person leaves behind while using the Internet, such as websites visited, posts and comments, searches, emails, photographs shared and online purchases. It is also called a digital shadow or digital tattoo because it is hard to erase.

blocks.caption: Active and passive digital footprint
rows: Active
The user deliberately shares the data
Posting on social media, sending an email, filling an online form, uploading a photo
Passive
Data is collected without the user actively submitting it
Browsing history, IP address, location, cookies, search history recorded by websites and apps

blocks.text: What to learn from this figure: A digital footprint is not only what you post. Data collected silently is part of it too, and the whole trail cannot be fully deleted, so share less and use privacy settings.
Because a footprint can be seen by employers, colleges and strangers and can be copied or shared further, a user should think before posting and should check the privacy settings of every account.
**Net etiquette (netiquette)** is the set of good manners to follow while using the Internet:

- Be respectful and polite; do not use abusive or offensive language, and do not write in all capital letters, which is read as shouting.
- Do not share personal information such as address, phone number, passwords or photos of others without permission.
- Respect copyright: give credit and do not copy or download pirated material.
- Avoid spreading rumours and unverified news; check the source before forwarding.
- Do not spam, send chain messages or post irrelevant content.
- Do not trouble, tease or harass others; accept differences of opinion calmly.

**Social media etiquette** applies the same ideas to chats and posts: take permission before tagging or posting a photograph of someone, think before you post because deleted posts may already have been copied, use group chats responsibly, and report abusive behaviour instead of replying to it.
The digital footprint cannot be fully deleted. The safest approach is to share less, control privacy settings and be polite online.
Passive does not mean harmless: cookies and location data collected silently are still part of the footprint, and many users forget that they exist.
Data protection and intellectual property rights

The practice of safeguarding important or personal information (such as identity details, bank data and health records) from loss, misuse, theft or unauthorised access, and of using it only for its stated purpose.

Measures include strong and unique passwords, two-factor authentication, encryption, regular backups, software updates, antivirus and firewall, and giving apps only the permissions they need. Organisations that collect personal data are expected to keep it secure and use it lawfully.

Legal rights given to the creator or owner over creations of the mind, such as inventions, literary and artistic works, designs, symbols, names and images used in commerce, so that others cannot use them without permission.

blocks.caption: Main kinds of intellectual property
rows: Copyright
Original literary, artistic, musical and dramatic works, films and software code; arises automatically when the work is created
A novel, a song, a photograph, a computer programme
Patent
A new invention or process; gives the inventor exclusive rights for a limited period (20 years in India) in return for disclosing the invention
A new type of engine or a new manufacturing process
Trademark
A word, name, logo, symbol or slogan that identifies the goods or services of a business
A company logo or brand name

blocks.text: **Violation of IPR** means using protected work without the owner permission. Examples: **copyright infringement** (copying or distributing books, music, films or software without permission, known as piracy), **trademark infringement** (using a similar logo or name to mislead buyers) and **patent infringement** (making or selling a patented invention without the right to do so).
Copyright protects the way an idea is expressed, not the idea itself, and a patent protects an invention, not a brand. A logo is a trademark, a song is a copyright.
Plagiarism, licensing, copyright, FOSS and Creative Commons

Presenting the words, ideas, images or work of someone else as your own without giving proper credit to the source. It is an unethical act, and copying a work that is protected by copyright may also be illegal.

Plagiarism includes copying text from the Internet into your project, submitting someone else assignment, and using pictures or code without acknowledging the creator. It can be avoided by writing in your own words, quoting with quotation marks and citing the source in a reference list or bibliography. Plagiarism checkers compare a text against a large database of existing material.
A legal agreement between the owner and the user that states how the software may be used, copied, modified and shared. Using software beyond its licence terms is a violation of the licence.

**Copyright** gives the creator the right to copy, distribute and adapt the work; others need the creator permission, usually in the form of a licence. **Proprietary software** (for example Microsoft Windows and Microsoft Office) is owned by a company; users receive only the right to use it and the source code is kept secret.

Software whose source code is available to everyone, who may use, study, modify and redistribute it. "Free" refers to freedom, not necessarily to price. Examples: Linux, the Python language, LibreOffice, GIMP and the Mozilla Firefox browser.

A non-profit organisation that provides standard free licences by which creators allow others to share and build on their work under stated conditions, summarised as "some rights reserved". Common conditions are Attribution (BY, give credit), NonCommercial (NC), NoDerivatives (ND, no changes) and ShareAlike (SA, share new work under the same licence).

blocks.caption: Proprietary software versus FOSS
rows: Source code
Hidden from the user
Open to everyone
Modification
Not allowed
Allowed
Cost
Usually paid (may be free to use)
Often free of cost but not necessarily
Examples
MS Office, Windows
Linux, LibreOffice, Python

blocks.text: Copyright is automatic; a licence (proprietary, FOSS or Creative Commons) tells others what they may do. The CC BY licence only requires that you give credit to the creator.
Free software is not the same as freeware. FOSS lets you see and change the source code; freeware is usually free of charge but its source code is not shared.
Cybercrime, cyber laws and the Indian IT Act
Any criminal activity in which a computer, a network or a digital device is the tool, the target or the place of the crime, for example fraud, identity theft and unauthorised access.

blocks.caption: Common cybercrimes
rows: Hacking

Gaining unauthorised access to a computer system or network and misusing data or system. An ethical (white-hat) hacker does this with permission to find and fix weaknesses; a malicious (black-hat) hacker does it for harm or gain
Breaking into a school database to alter grades
Phishing
Sending fake emails, messages or websites that look genuine, to trick a user into revealing sensitive information such as passwords, OTP or card details
An email that pretends to be from a bank and asks you to click a link and enter your PIN
Cyberbullying
Harassing, threatening, humiliating or embarrassing a person using digital media such as messages, social media or chat
Sending hurtful messages or posting an insulting photograph of a classmate
Identity theft
Using someone else personal information to commit fraud
Opening an account with another person identity details

blocks.text: The branch of law that deals with the use of computers, the Internet and electronic data, covering cybercrime, electronic records, digital signatures and online conduct.

**Indian IT Act (Information Technology Act, 2000)** is the main Indian law on cyber matters. It gives legal recognition to electronic records and digital signatures, which makes electronic contracts and e-governance valid, and it defines cyber offences such as unauthorised access to computers, damaging data, identity theft and cheating using computers, together with their penalties. The Act was amended in 2008 to cover new kinds of cybercrime. Cybercrime victims can complain to the police or through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal.

blocks.problem: A student receives an email that says "Your bank account will be blocked. Click this link and enter your card number and OTP immediately." Identify the cybercrime and state two precautions.
blocks.solution:
The email pretends to be from the bank and asks for confidential details through a link. This is **phishing**.

Precautions: (1) do not click on links in unexpected messages; (2) never share OTP, PIN or card details; (3) check the sender address and contact the bank through its official website or number.
blocks.answer: Phishing; do not click the link, do not share OTP or PIN, verify with the bank directly.

blocks.problem: A school magazine wants to use a poster licensed as CC BY-NC-ND. Can the magazine (a) print it with the artist name, (b) crop and recolour it, (c) use it on a page that sells advertisements?
blocks.solution:
CC BY means the user must give credit to the creator; NC means no commercial use; ND means no changes may be made.

(a) Printing the poster unchanged with the artist name satisfies BY and ND, and a non-profit school magazine satisfies NC, so it is allowed.

(b) Cropping and recolouring is a change, which ND forbids, so it is not allowed.

(c) Selling advertisements around it is a commercial use, which NC forbids, so it is not allowed.

blocks.text: Preventing cybercrime
Cybercrime can be reduced by habits and tools:

- Use strong, unique passwords and enable two-factor authentication.
- Install and update the operating system, browser and antivirus software regularly.
- Do not click on unknown links or open unexpected attachments; check that a site address begins with https before entering sensitive data.
- Do not share OTP, PIN or passwords with anyone, and avoid doing banking over open public Wi-Fi.
- Keep social media accounts private, and block and report people who bully.
- Take regular backups of important data, and report cybercrime to the police or the cyber crime portal without delay.
The most effective protection against phishing is user awareness: no genuine bank asks for your PIN or OTP over email, message or call.
E-waste: hazards and management
Discarded electrical and electronic equipment that is old, broken or no longer wanted, such as computers, mobile phones, batteries, televisions, printers and chargers.

**Hazards.** E-waste contains toxic materials such as lead, mercury, cadmium and brominated flame retardants. If it is dumped in landfills the toxic substances can seep into soil and groundwater, and burning cables and plastics in the open releases poisonous fumes. Workers handling it without protection may suffer damage to the nervous system, kidneys, lungs and skin; the environment and food chain are polluted.

**Management.** The following steps are used:

- **Reduce:** buy only what you need and prefer long-lasting devices.
- **Reuse:** repair, upgrade, donate or resell a working device.
- **Recycle:** hand over e-waste to authorised recyclers who recover valuable metals safely.
- Return old devices through manufacturer take-back or buy-back schemes and e-waste collection centres; never throw them in household garbage.
- India has E-Waste (Management) Rules which make producers responsible for collecting and recycling the e-waste of their products.
Burning e-waste to recover metals is not a safe form of recycling because it releases toxic fumes. Recycling must be done by authorised recyclers.
Health concerns and ergonomics
Long use of computers and phones can affect health:

blocks.caption: Health effects and remedies
rows: Eye strain (digital eye strain), dryness, headache, blurred vision
Staring at a screen for a long time, glare, wrong brightness, blinking less
Follow the 20-20-20 rule (every 20 minutes look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds), blink often, adjust brightness, reduce glare
Neck, shoulder and back pain
Poor sitting posture, bending the neck to look at a phone
Sit upright with back support, keep the screen at eye level, take short walks
Repetitive strain injury and wrist pain (carpal tunnel)
Typing or using a mouse for long periods with the wrist bent
Keep wrists straight, use a wrist rest, take breaks and stretch
Sleep disturbance, tiredness, little physical activity
Using screens late at night, sitting for long hours
Avoid screens before bed and exercise regularly
Stress, anxiety and screen addiction
Overuse of games and social media
Limit screen time and spend time with family and outdoors

blocks.text: The study of designing the workplace, furniture and equipment so that they suit the human body and reduce strain, discomfort and injury.

Ergonomic set-up: the chair should have back support and the feet should rest flat on the floor; the top of the monitor should be at or slightly below eye level, about an arm length away; the keyboard and mouse should be at elbow height so that the wrists remain straight; the room lighting should not cause glare on the screen.
Take a short break after every 30 to 60 minutes of continuous screen use, and keep the screen at or slightly below eye level at about an arm length.

diagrams.alt: Two panels, active footprint with posts, emails and forms, and passive footprint with cookies, location data and IP address, with arrows to a box labelled digital footprint
diagrams.caption: Active and passive digital footprint
diagrams.description: An active footprint is data you share on purpose: posts, emails and forms. A passive footprint is collected without your action: cookies, location data, IP address and browsing history. Together they make up your digital footprint.

questions.stem: Posting a photograph on a social media site is an example of which kind of digital footprint?
questions.explanation: An active digital footprint is the data a user deliberately shares, such as posts, comments, emails and uploaded photographs. A passive footprint is collected without the user actively submitting it, for example browsing history or the IP address. Hardware footprint and copyright footprint are not standard terms.

optionRationale.1: A passive footprint is gathered silently, for example cookies and IP address.
optionRationale.3: Hardware footprint is not a type of digital footprint.
optionRationale.4: Copyright footprint is not a term used for the trail of user data.

questions.stem: A fraudulent email that looks like it comes from a bank and asks the user to enter a PIN on a fake website is an example of
questions.explanation: Phishing uses fake messages or websites that imitate a trusted organisation to trick people into revealing confidential information such as passwords, PINs and OTPs. Hacking is unauthorised access to systems; cyberbullying is harassment and plagiarism is copying work.

optionRationale.1: Hacking means gaining unauthorised access to a system, not tricking a user into giving details.
optionRationale.2: Cyberbullying is harassment through digital media.
optionRationale.3: Plagiarism is presenting someone else work as your own.

questions.stem: Presenting another person work or ideas as your own without acknowledging the source is called
questions.explanation: Plagiarism means using someone else words, ideas or creations as your own without giving credit. It can be avoided by writing in your own words and citing the sources. Hacking and phishing are cybercrimes involving access and deception.

optionRationale.2: Hacking is unauthorised access to computer systems.
optionRationale.3: Phishing tricks users to reveal confidential data.
optionRationale.4: This is not a term in the syllabus and does not describe copying ideas.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of Free and Open-Source Software?
questions.explanation: LibreOffice has publicly available source code that anyone may use, study, modify and share, so it is FOSS. Microsoft Office, Adobe Photoshop and Windows are proprietary products whose source code is not released.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an ergonomic habit that helps prevent eye strain?
options: Reading in a dark room on a bright screen
Keeping the screen as close to the eyes as possible
Not blinking while watching the screen
Looking at an object 20 feet away for 20 seconds after every 20 minutes of screen work
questions.explanation: The 20-20-20 rule lets the eye muscles relax and reduces dryness and tiredness. The other habits (dark room with a bright screen, very close screen, reduced blinking) increase strain on the eyes.

optionRationale.1: A dark room with a bright screen increases glare and strain.
optionRationale.2: A very close screen increases eye strain.
optionRationale.3: Blinking less dries the eyes and increases strain.

questions.stem: Which type of intellectual property protects the logo and brand name of a company?
questions.explanation: A trademark protects words, names, logos and symbols that identify the goods or services of a business. Copyright protects original creative works, and a patent protects an invention. A licence is permission to use something.

optionRationale.1: Copyright protects works such as books, songs and software code.
optionRationale.3: A patent protects a new invention, not a brand name.
optionRationale.4: A licence is an agreement to use a work; it is not a type of property right.

questions.stem: A user downloads a song and shares it with friends without the permission of the owner. This is an example of
questions.explanation: Copying or distributing a copyrighted song, film, book or software without the owner permission violates copyright and is called piracy. Trademark registration and patent filing are legal ways of protecting property, and a digital signature authenticates an electronic document.

optionRationale.1: Registering a trademark is a legal step by the owner, not a violation.
optionRationale.2: Filing a patent is a legal step for protecting an invention.
optionRationale.4: A digital signature verifies the sender of an electronic record.

questions.stem: Under which Creative Commons condition must the user give credit to the original creator?
questions.explanation: Attribution (BY) requires every user to give credit to the creator. NC bars commercial use, ND bars changes to the work and SA requires that new works be shared under the same licence.

optionRationale.2: NC restricts commercial use of the work.
optionRationale.4: SA requires derivative works to carry the same licence.

questions.stem: Which statement about e-waste is correct?
options: Old computers and phones should be given to authorised recyclers because they contain toxic substances such as lead and mercury.
E-waste is harmless and can be thrown with household garbage.
Burning e-waste in the open is the safest way to recover metals.
Only large machines such as TVs are called e-waste.
questions.explanation: E-waste includes all discarded electronic devices, big or small, and contains toxic substances such as lead, mercury and cadmium. These must be handled by authorised recyclers; open burning releases harmful fumes and dumping contaminates soil and water.

optionRationale.2: E-waste contains toxic materials and must not be mixed with household garbage.
optionRationale.3: Open burning releases toxic fumes and is unsafe.
optionRationale.4: Phones, batteries and chargers also count as e-waste.

questions.stem: Rina sets her social media profile to private, avoids sharing her phone number and asks friends before tagging her. Which concept does this best illustrate?
options: Managing her digital footprint and data privacy
questions.explanation: Using privacy settings, limiting personal information and controlling what others post about her are ways of managing the digital footprint and protecting personal data. None of the actions involve copying work, tricking users or pirating software.

optionRationale.1: Plagiarism is copying work without credit.
optionRationale.2: Phishing is a crime committed against users.
optionRationale.4: Software piracy is illegal copying of software.

questions.stem:
Statements:
A. A patent gives exclusive rights over an invention for a limited period.
B. FOSS means the software must always be free of charge.
C. Cyberbullying involves harassing a person using digital media.
D. Copyright is protected only after the work is registered and stops in the absence of a licence.
Which are correct?
questions.explanation: A is true: a patent is a time-limited exclusive right. C is true by definition. B is false because "free" in FOSS means freedom to use, study and modify the source code, not necessarily price. D is false since copyright arises automatically on creation. So A and C only.

optionRationale.1: B is false, so this option containing B is incorrect.
optionRationale.3: B and D are both false.
optionRationale.4: D is false, so this option is incorrect.

questions.objective: Evaluate statements on IPR and cyber issues

questions.stem: Which of the following is a passive digital footprint?
options: A comment that you posted on a video
An email that you sent to your teacher
A form that you filled in with your name
Your browsing history and IP address recorded by a website
questions.explanation: Passive footprints are collected without the user deliberately submitting them, such as the IP address, browsing history and cookies. The comment, email and form are all things the user knowingly sends or posts, so they are active.

optionRationale.1: A posted comment is deliberately shared.
optionRationale.2: An email is deliberately sent by the user.
optionRationale.3: A form is deliberately filled by the user.

questions.stem: A student copies three paragraphs from a website into her project, changes a few words and does not mention the website. Which statement is most accurate?
options: It is not plagiarism because the website is public.
It is phishing because the website text was taken.
It is plagiarism, and she should have paraphrased properly and cited the source.
It is allowed because the project is not sold.
questions.explanation: Using someone else text without credit is plagiarism, even if a few words are changed and even if the website is freely visible. The remedy is to write in her own words, put quoted text in quotation marks and list the source. Phishing is a deception crime and unrelated.

optionRationale.1: A page being public does not remove the creator rights or the need to give credit.
optionRationale.2: Phishing is a different crime that tricks people into giving information.
optionRationale.4: Plagiarism does not depend on selling the work.

questions.objective: Apply the concept of plagiarism to a case

questions.stem: A blogger uses a photograph licensed as CC BY-NC in an advertisement for her paid online store and does not mention the photographer. Which licence conditions does she break?
options: None, because Creative Commons works can be used in any way
questions.explanation: CC BY requires giving credit to the creator, and NC forbids commercial use. An advertisement for a paid store is commercial, and she gave no credit, so both Attribution and NonCommercial are broken. ND and SA are not part of this licence.

optionRationale.2: The photograph was not altered, and ND is not part of the licence in any case.
optionRationale.3: SA is not a condition of this licence.
optionRationale.4: Creative Commons licences are free to use only under the stated conditions.

questions.objective: Apply Creative Commons conditions to a case

questions.stem: Which pair correctly matches the crime with its description?
options: Hacking: copying a research article without credit
Phishing: unauthorised access to a computer by guessing the password
Plagiarism: sending fake emails to collect bank details
Cyberbullying: sending repeated hurtful messages to humiliate a person online
questions.explanation: Cyberbullying is harassment or humiliation of a person through digital media. Copying a research article without credit is plagiarism, guessing a password to enter a system is hacking and fake emails for bank details are phishing, so the other pairs are mismatched.

questions.stem: The Information Technology Act, 2000 of India primarily
options: prohibits the use of the Internet by students
gives legal recognition to electronic records and digital signatures and defines cyber offences and penalties
deals only with patents on software
questions.explanation: The IT Act, 2000 provides the legal framework for electronic records, digital signatures and e-commerce, and lists offences such as unauthorised access and identity theft with penalties. It was amended in 2008. It does not ban Internet use or FOSS and does not deal with patents.

optionRationale.1: The Act does not ban Internet use.
optionRationale.3: Patents are covered by a separate law.
optionRationale.4: The Act does not make FOSS illegal.

questions.objective: State the scope of the IT Act

questions.stem: Which ergonomic set-up is best for a student working on a desktop computer?
options: Back bent forward, feet hanging, screen far above eye level, wrists bent upward
Back supported, feet flat on floor, screen top at or just below eye level, wrists straight
Lying down with the keyboard on the stomach
Screen kept very close to the face with bright overhead glare
questions.explanation: Ergonomics aims to keep the body in a neutral posture: supported back, feet on the floor, monitor near eye level an arm length away, and straight wrists. The other options cause neck, back, wrist and eye strain.

optionRationale.1: A bent back, high screen and bent wrists cause strain.
optionRationale.3: Lying down gives poor support and wrist posture.
optionRationale.4: A very close, glaring screen strains the eyes.

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Giving credit to the original author is necessary while using material taken from a website.
Reason (R): Using another person work without acknowledgement amounts to plagiarism.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Acknowledging the source is the way to avoid plagiarism, which is presenting another person work as your own. The reason therefore explains exactly why credit is necessary. In short, acknowledging the source is how a user avoids plagiarism.

optionRationale.2: R is the direct reason for A.
optionRationale.3: R is true, so the option stating R is false is wrong.
optionRationale.4: A is true, so the option stating A is false is wrong.

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): FOSS software is always free of cost.
Reason (R): FOSS allows users to access, modify and share the source code.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: The assertion is false: "free" in FOSS means freedom, and a company may charge for support, distribution or services. The reason is true because FOSS gives access to the source code with rights to change and share it. So A is false and R is true.

optionRationale.1: A is false, so options with A true are wrong.
optionRationale.2: A is false, so this option is wrong.
optionRationale.3: A is false, so this option is wrong.

questions.objective: Distinguish free software from free of cost

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): A person with no social media posts can still have a digital footprint.
Reason (R): Websites record the IP address and browsing activity of visitors.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Passive footprints such as the IP address, cookies and browsing history are recorded by websites even if the user posts nothing. Hence the assertion is true and the reason is exactly why.

optionRationale.3: R is true, so R is false option is wrong.
optionRationale.4: A is true, so A false option is wrong.

questions.stem: Match the term in List-I with the matching description in List-II.
questions.explanation: Phishing (A) is tricking users to reveal information with fake messages (III). Hacking (B) is unauthorised access to a system (IV). A patent (C) is an exclusive right over an invention (I). A trademark (D) protects brand names and logos (II). The code is A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II.

optionRationale.1: This swaps phishing and patent descriptions.
optionRationale.2: This gives hacking the brand-protection description.

right: I. Exclusive right over an invention for a limited time
II. Protects brand names and logos
III. Fake messages used to obtain confidential details
IV. Unauthorised access to a computer system
